@@132679970 <p> Caroline Muller looks at clouds differently than most people . Where others may see puffy marshmallows , wispy cotton candy or thunderous gray objects storming overhead , Muller sees fluids flowing through the sky . She visualizes how air rises and falls , warms and cools , and spirals and swirls to form clouds and create storms . <p> But the urgency with which Muller , a climate scientist at the Institute of Science and Technology Austria in Klosterneuburg , considers such atmospheric puzzles has surged in recent years . As our planet swelters with global warming , storms are becoming more intense , sometimes dumping two or even three times more rain than expected . Such was the case in Bah ? a Blanca , Argentina , in March 2025 : Almost half the city 's yearly average rainfall fell in less than 12 hours , causing deadly floods . <p> Atmospheric scientists have long used computer simulations to track how the dynamics of air and moisture might produce varieties of storms . But existing models had n't fully explained the emergence of these fiercer storms . A @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ than cooler air : an extra 7 percent for every degree Celsius of warming . But in models and weather observations , climate scientists have seen rainfall events far exceeding this expected increase . And those storms can lead to severe flooding when heavy rain falls on already saturated soils or follows humid heatwaves . <p> Clouds , and the way that they cluster , could help explain what 's going on . <p> A growing body of research , set in motion by Muller over a decade ago , is revealing several small-scale processes that climate models had previously overlooked . These processes influence how clouds form , congregate , and persist in ways that may amplify heavy downpours and fuel larger , long-lasting storms . Clouds have an " internal life , " Muller says , " that can strengthen them or may help them stay alive longer . " <p> Other scientists need more convincing , because the computer simulations researchers use to study clouds reduce planet Earth to its simplest and smoothest form , retaining its essential physics but otherwise barely resembling the real world . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Higher-resolution global climate models can finally simulate clouds and the destructive storms they form on a planetary scale -- giving scientists a more realistic picture . By better understanding clouds , researchers hope to improve their predictions of extreme rainfall , especially in the tropics where some of the most ferocious thunderstorms hit and where future rainfall projections are the most uncertain . <h> First clues to clumping clouds <p> All clouds form in moist , rising air . A mountain can propel air upward ; so , too , can a cold front . Clouds can also form through a process known as convection : the overturning of air in the atmosphere that starts when sunlight , warm land or balmy water heats air from below . As warm air rises , it cools , condensing the water vapor it carried upwards into raindrops . This condensation process also releases heat , which fuels churning storms . <p> But clouds remain one of the weakest links in climate models . That 's because the global climate models scientists use to simulate scenarios of future warming are far too coarse @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to describe how they swirl in a storm -- let alone to explain the microphysical processes controlling how much rain falls from them to Earth . <p> To try to resolve this problem , Muller and other like-minded scientists turned to simpler simulations of Earth 's climate that are able to model convection . In these artificial worlds , each the shape of a shallow box typically a few hundred kilometers across and tens of kilometers deep , the researchers tinkered with replica atmospheres to see if they could figure out how clouds behaved under different conditions . <p> The top frame of this computer simulation shows an atmosphere where the movements of air are somewhat disorganized , leading to clouds popping up in random locations . At the bottom is a simulation of an atmosphere where patterns of convection have become organized , and clouds spontaneously clump together into one large region -- forming a storm . <p> Intriguingly , when researchers ran these models , the clouds spontaneously clumped together , even though the models had none of the features that usually push clouds together -- no mountains @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in sunlight . " Nobody knew why this was happening , " says Daniel Hern ? ndez Deckers , an atmospheric scientist at the National University of Colombia in Bogot ? . <p> In 2012 , Muller discovered a first clue : a process known as radiative cooling . The Sun 's heat that bounces off Earth 's surface radiates back into space , and where there are few clouds , more of that radiation escapes -- cooling the air . The cool spots set up atmospheric flows that drive air toward cloudier regions -- trapping more heat and forming more clouds . A follow-up study in 2018 showed that in these simulations , radiative cooling accelerated the formation of tropical cyclones . " That made us realize that to understand clouds , you have to look at the neighborhood as well -- outside clouds , " Muller says . <p> Once scientists started looking not just outside clouds , but also underneath them and at their edges , they found other small-scale processes that help to explain why clouds flock together . The various processes , described by Muller @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ all bring or hold together pockets of warm , moist air so more clouds form in already-cloudy regions . These small-scale processes had n't been understood much before because they are often obscured by larger weather patterns . <p> Hern ? ndez Deckers has been studying one of the processes , called entrainment -- the turbulent mixing of air at the edges of clouds . Most climate models represent clouds as a steady plume of rising air , but in reality " clouds are like a cauliflower , " he says . " You have a lot of turbulence , and you have these bubbles of air inside the clouds . " This mixing at the edges affects how clouds evolve and thunderstorms develop ; it can weaken or strengthen storms in various ways , but , like radiative cooling , it encourages more clouds to form as a clump in regions that are already moist . <p> Such processes are likely to be most important in storms in Earth 's tropical regions , where there 's the most uncertainty about future rainfall . ( That 's why Hern ? @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ their studies there . ) The tropics lack the cold fronts , jet streams , and spiraling high- and low-pressure systems that dominate air flows at higher latitudes . <h> Supercharging heavy rains <p> There are other microscopic processes happening inside clouds that affect extreme rainfall , especially on shorter timescales . Moisture matters : Condensed droplets falling through moist , cloudy air do n't evaporate as much on their descent , so more water falls to the ground . Temperature matters too : When clouds form in warmer atmospheres , they produce less snow and more rain . Since raindrops fall faster than snowflakes , they evaporate less on their descent -- producing , once again , more rain . <p> These factors also help explain why more rain can get squeezed from a cloud than the 7 percent rise per degree of warming predicted by the 200-year-old theory . " Essentially you get an extra kick ... in our simulations , it was almost a doubling , " says Martin Singh , a climate scientist at Monash University in Melbourne , Australia . <p> Cloud clustering adds to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ so more rain droplets fall . One study by Muller and her collaborators found that clumping clouds intensify short-duration rainfall extremes by 30 to 70 percent , largely because raindrops evaporate less inside sodden clouds . <p> Other research , including a study led by Jiawei Bao , a postdoctoral researcher in Muller 's group , has likewise found that the microphysical processes going on inside clouds have a strong influence over fast , heavy downpours . These sudden downpours are intensifying much faster with climate change than protracted deluges , and often cause flash flooding . <h> The future of extreme rainfall <p> Scientists who study the clumping of clouds want to know how that behavior will change as the planet heats up -- and what that will mean for incidences of heavy rainfall and flooding . <p> Some models suggest that clouds ( and the convection that gives rise to them ) will clump together more with global warming -- and produce more rainfall extremes that often far exceed what theory predicts . But other simulations suggest that clouds will congregate less . " There seems to be @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Wing , a climate scientist at Florida State University in Tallahassee who has compared various models . <p> Scientists are beginning to try to reconcile some of these inconsistencies using powerful types of computer simulations called global storm-resolving models . These can capture the fine structures of clouds , thunderstorms , and cyclones while also simulating the global climate . They bring a 50-fold leap in realism beyond the global climate models scientists generally use -- but demand 30,000 times more computational power . <p> Using one such model in a paper published in 2024 , Bao , Muller , and their collaborators found that clouds in the tropics congregated more as temperatures increased -- leading to less frequent storms but ones that were larger , lasted longer , and , over the course of a day , dumped more rain than expected from theory . <p> But that work relied on just one model and simulated conditions from around one future time point -- the year 2070 . Scientists need to run longer simulations using more storm-resolving models , Bao says , but very few research teams can afford @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ they are typically run at large centralized hubs , and scientists occasionally host " hackathons " to crunch through and share data . <p> Researchers also need more real-world observations to get at some of the biggest unknowns about clouds . Although a flurry of recent studies using satellite data linked the clustering of clouds to heavier rainfall in the tropics , there are large data gaps in many tropical regions . This weakens climate projections and leaves many countries ill-prepared . In June of 2025 , floods and landslides in Venezuela and Colombia swept away buildings and killed at least a dozen people , but scientists do n't know what factors worsened these storms because the data are so paltry . " Nobody really knows , still , what triggered this , " Hern ? ndez Deckers says . <p> New , granular data are on their way . Wing is analyzing rainfall measurements from a German research vessel that traversed the tropical Atlantic Ocean for six weeks in 2024 . The ship 's radar mapped clusters of convection associated with the storms it passed through , so the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ tracts of the ocean . <p> And an even more global view is on the horizon . The European Space Agency plans to launch two satellites in 2029 that will measure , among other things , near-surface winds that ruffle Earth 's oceans and skim mountaintops . Perhaps , scientists hope , the data these satellites beam back will finally provide a better grasp of clumping clouds and the heaviest rains that fall from them . <p> Research and interviews for this article were partly supported through a journalism residency funded by the Institute of Science &amp; Technology Austria ( ISTA ) . @@132679977 <p> On May 29 , 2014 , some 30,000 guests streamed through the university 's wrought-iron gates and into Harvard Yard , settling into rows of folding chairs . The sound of church bells floated through the air , and the pageantry of the 363rd commencement unfolded in ritual calm . <p> " Mr. Sheriff , pray give us order ! " said the university marshal , in accordance with tradition . The sheriff of Middlesex County , wearing a silk top hat , banged a cane on the stage three times . " The meeting will be in order ! " <p> Harvard did n't have just any singer perform " The Star-Spangled Banner " that day , it had Aretha Franklin , the queen of soul herself . Michael Bloomberg , the billionaire former mayor of New York City , had prepared a keynote speech . Alan Garber , Harvard 's provost at the time , would award an honorary doctorate to 89-year-old George H.W. Bush , the former Republican president . <p> Amid the sea of caps and gowns , the faces of the Class of 2014 told a story of transformation . An institution once reserved exclusively for the sons of New England 's Brahmin elite was sending off one of its most diverse classes ever . Women made up 47 percent of the more than 1,600 seniors ; 54 percent of the graduates were Black , Latino , Asian-American , multiracial , or hailed from abroad . <p> University leaders prized the school'sdiversity -- not least president Drew Faust , Harvard 's first female president . It was a sign they were training the next generation of global leaders . <p> By some measures , Harvard had already cornered that market . The university had produced 160 Nobel Prize laureates , over 100 billionaires , and eight US presidents -- Harvard Law grad Barack Obama was then well into his second term . <p> " We were the generation of hope , " recalled Yolanda Borquaye , who led the Association of Black Harvard Women and graduated that day . <p> A special commencement program celebrated Harvard scholars making breakthroughs in science and medicine , leading in education and the arts , and fighting poverty . Donations from across the political spectrum were pouring in from alumni , including multimillion dollar gifts from two billionaire hedge fund managers , Bill Ackman of New York and Ken Griffin of Chicago . The university was running nearly 900 research projects around the world . <p> " Harvard is making a difference now , " the program said , " and is working to lead the way in the next decade . " <p> Few at the 2014 commencement could have predicted that , a decade later , President Trump would target Harvard with the most severe set ofsanctions ever imposed on a major university , casting it and other elite institutions as radical forces undermining America . Fewer still could have anticipated how Harvard 's confrontation with Trump would reflect the nation 's own conflicts over who we are and what we want to stand for . <p> One person at commencement did see ominous warnings , however : Bloomberg , who was raised nearby in working-class Medford . That afternoon , he stepped to the podium to deliver a somewhat unusual speech for a happy occasion . " There is no easy time to say hard things , " he said . <p> Bloomberg had been observing escalating rancor in Congress and the political undermining of science and research expertise . On college campuses , there were other worrying trends : invitations to conservative speakers rescinded after student protests , the shaming of professors whose views violated progressive norms , and colleges becoming liberal echo chambers . <p> " Think about the irony , " Bloomberg said . " In the 1950s , the right wing was attempting to repress left-wing ideas . Today , on many college campuses , it is liberals trying to repress conservative ideas , even as conservative faculty members are at risk of becoming an endangered species . " <p> Bloomberg challenged students to fight the urge to shout down people with different views . Higher education is " perpetually vulnerable to the tyrannical tendencies of monarchs , mobs , and majorities , " he warned . <p> And the winds of politics have a way of shifting quickly . <p> Aretha Franklin , Michael Bloomberg , and George H.W. Bush at the 2014 Harvard commencement , where they all received honorary degrees . ( Lane Turner/Globe Staff ) <p> Bloomberg 's speech might have been more prophetic than even he intended . <p> Five months later , the US midterm elections delivered a historic red wave . Republicans regained control of the Senate and strengthened their House majority to a level not seen in nearly a century . Among the House freshmen was 30-year-old Elise Stefanik , a Harvard alumna and , at the time , the youngest woman ever elected to Congress . In a decade , she 'd help lead a battle against the college that educated her . <p> Then there was Donald Trump . <p> Two days before Harvard 's 2014 commencement , the real estate magnate and reality show star was the featured guest at the National Press Club luncheon , not far from the White House . <p> He had been watching the Tea Party gaining strength , calling for a political reckoning in Washington . In his speech , he lingered on some of his favorite themes . Obama 's birth certificate . His talent for building brands and crushing foes on Twitter . How America 's economy was a loser compared to China . <p> " It 's about winning , " Trump said , no fewer than seven times in his talk . <p> Trump was asked why he had n't run for president . " If I do n't see the right person I will do something in ' 16 , " he vowed . " I will do it as sure as you 're sitting here . " <h> Why Harvard ? <p> How the world 's most powerful university found itself under brutal attack by the world 's most powerful man will be debated for years . <p> Was President Trump 's decisionto freeze more than$2 billion of Harvard 's federal research funding , threaten its ability to bring in foreign students , and impose a slew of other sanctions just a power play ? A media-obsessed president relishing the spectacle of going after the nation 's most famous college ? <p> But for others , that explanation overlooks a deeper reality . When Trump turned his fire on Harvard , vast swaths of the country went along . Many Americans even cheered . <p> How did Harvard find itself in this position ? Since the summer , Globe reporters have studied this question , poring over legal filings , research reports , and campus surveys , and speaking with more than 150 people , including Harvard administrators , faculty , alumni , students , higher-education leaders , and public officials . Many declined to be named because of ongoing negotiations between Harvard and the White House . <p> There are no simple answers , only a collage of overlapping narratives that shared one theme : Over the past decade , as political and cultural upheavals fractured the nation , and social media intensified every divide , Harvard became the university that plenty of everyday Americans loved to hate . <p> Trump was determined to attack the elites , and Harvard had a bullseye on its back . ( Video : Randy Vazquez/Globe staff , Photo : Jessica Rinaldi/Globe staff ) <p> Harvard 's leaders say they have strived to be on the right side of history , guided by the school 's motto " Veritas , " the Latin word for truth . They embraced the values of multiculturalism and international engagement as integral to a 21st century education . Students and faculty who leaned into this decade 's major social movements -- such as Black Lives Matter , MeToo , LGBTQ rights -- were seen as positively engaging with the nation and the world . <p> But during this period , Harvard paid less attention to other issues , including a growing intolerance on campus for any views that might seem to challenge its egalitarian mission . Students and professors alike became increasingly afraid of speaking their minds , especially if their ideas clashed with the progressive ethos . By 2024 , Harvard found two out of three graduating seniors feared sharing their beliefs about controversial subjects in class . <p> While Harvard was embracing the ideals of racial justice and global involvement over this decade , many Americans outside the university 's ivy-clad walls were turning away from those values . Or perhaps had never supported them in the first place . A conservative narrative rose that Harvard was full of itself and worse , in ways undermining what was best for America . <p> Lawrence Bacow bristles at that notion . During his Harvard presidency , between 2018 and 2023 , he helped commission military cadets in the ROTC program . " I would remind them that Harvard was 140 years old when the Declaration of Independence was signed , " Bacow recalled . Eight Harvard alumni signed it , and five were framers of the US Constitution . <p> Advertisement <p> " My point was that Harvard literally helped to bring this country into being , " he told the Globe . " So this notion that we do n't care about our country -- it 's just , as you can tell , it gets my blood boiling . " <p> The crisis of trust in higher education extended well beyond Harvard . From 2015 to 2023 , the percentage of Americans who expressed high confidence in colleges and universities collapsed from 57 percent to 36 percent , according to Gallup . But the nation 's most famous university was bound to attract the bulk of the negative attention . <p> From 2014 to 2025 , Harvard coverage on Fox News far surpassed any other top 20 university in the US News &amp; World Report rankings , according to a Globe review . Harvard was the subject of more than 300 stories -- nearly twice as many as Columbia University , the second most covered -- and almost all of them framed as examples of liberal excess . <p> Higher education 's costs were also soaring , and Harvard , with its $57 billion endowment , was the gilded example : Though it offers generous financial aid packages , Harvard charges $87,000 a year for its undergraduate education . That sticker price is bigger than the median annual household income in the US . And the college , which rejected 96 percent of its 50,000 or so applicants this year , continues to give admission boosts to children of alumni , known as legacies . <p> Could Harvard have done anything to dodge the worst of Trump 's attacks ? Many would say absolutely not -- he was always going to go after the biggest brand in college . But others saw how vulnerabilities developed over years made the university a perfect target for a president like Trump . <p> Rakesh Khurana was dean of Harvard College from 2014 through this past summer , and central to many of Harvard 's efforts to bridge divides over race , class , and politics . A sociologist by training , he now teaches at the college and Harvard Business School . <p> Professor Rakesh Khurana , shown at Harvard Business School , served as dean of Harvard College from 2014 through this summer . ( Craig F. Walker/Globe Staff ) <p> In interviews this fall , he paused when asked how Harvard found itself in this crisis with Trump . There are no simple answers , he said , but he offered an analogy : the fires that swept through Los Angeles earlier this year . <p> " Everybody 's like : ' Was it a match ? ' ' Was it a lightning strike ? ' " Khurana said . But what sparked the fires is only part of the story ; the other part is what allowed the flames to spread . " You also have all these houses built up close , " he said . " You have climate change , so it 's so dry now . You have the Santa Ana winds . You have buildings that are not up to code . " <p> " Until you take care of the conditions that set you up for that awful event , " Khurana said , " it 's going to happen again . " <p> Trump lit the match at Harvard , there 's no doubt about that . But before he did , the university 's leaders knew they had conditions on campus that needed to change . <h> Viral moments <p> In the spring of 2016 , as trees sprouted leaves outside her office in Harvard Yard , Faust was about to enter her 10th year as president . She was contemplating when to step down , yet still wrestling with a troubling piece of unfinished business : how to ensure students of all backgrounds felt supported by the university . <p> Faust had lived through tumultuous periods of change in her own life . A civil rights champion raised in the segregated South , she was deeply committed to the pluralistic ideal of America . She saw that bringing a broad range of students to Cambridge -- people of different races and religions , of different economic backgrounds , from different countries -- forged better ideas and a stronger education for everyone . <p> This environment produced robust debate and sometimes led to participation in the school 's history of campus activism , including large-scale protests against the Vietnam War , South Africa 's apartheid regime , and America 's income inequality . <p> " Out of that unruliness comes the odd idea that may change the world , " Faust said . <h> A changing Harvard campus <p> In 2016 , the campus was the most racially and ethnically diverse it had ever been . Because the size of Harvard 's undergraduate class had stayed the same for decades , white students made up a smaller proportion : 41 percent of Harvard 's American undergrads identified as white that year , roughly half of the percentage in 1980 , according to government data . <p> The decrease in white students produced other demographic shifts . About 10 percent of Harvard undergraduates were Jewish in 2016 , down from roughly 20 to 25 percent in the 1980s , student surveys show . The population of Muslims , Hindus , and Buddhists was growing , but still small -- about 5 percent collectively . <p> Harvard leaders could tell the air between students sometimes felt charged . " These differences could create stresses and tensions , " Faust recalled . " There were outcomes we had , in some cases , not fully anticipated . " <p> In 2012 , for example , 20-year-old junior Sarah Siskind touched off a campus controversy by publishing an op-ed in the Harvard Crimson , the student newspaper , that criticized affirmative action admissions policies based on race . Siskind , a libertarian , started out light -- joking there was no special boost for other disadvantaged groups like short or dumb people -- and then got more serious . <p> Siskind was concerned about the drawbacks of giving certain groups special advantages . She admitted she was a legacy applicant and worried she 'd taken a spot from a more deserving student . And she suggested all students admitted under more lenient standards might be regarded with " greater skepticism " by future employers . " Racism persists , despite over a century of incredible progress , " she wrote , " but affirmative action imbeds racism in the lives of future generations . " <p> To some students of color , the column was a personal affront , denying how amply qualified they were at a school that relied on multiple criteria for admission . <p> In a response published in the Crimson , Borquaye and two other leaders of Black student groups also explained how racism was inescapable for them no matter where they went . " Minorities can expect to experience racially prejudiced interactions in almost every part of their daily lives , regardless of their elevated socio-economic or educational statuses , " they wrote . <p> Sarah Siskind , a 2014 graduate of Harvard College , with her senior thesis adviser , Prof. Harvey Mansfield . Photo taken while she was an undergraduate . <p> In May 2014 , Yolanda Borquaye , a graduating senior from Georgia , spoke at a special commencement event at Cabot House at Harvard . <p> The dispute spread across campus , but not beyond . Social media in 2012was still mostly used by people to post birthday photos or bond over shared interests . " I would definitely have been canceled if it happened now , " Siskind said recently . <p> Now a science and comedy writer in New York City , she does n't regret publishing the column , but she wishes she could rewrite it to more fully recognize inequalities in educational opportunities . " I would be less flippant , " she said . <p> Some Harvard faculty turned the campus controversy into a teaching moment , organizing discussion forums that included the two women , who ended up on friendly terms as a result . It felt like there were more opportunities for productive " consciousness raising " in those days , said Borquaye , now a lawyer in London . <p> " We had more civil discourse then because it was more often in person , " she said . " I feel a bit of nostalgia for that time because we were n't all glued to our phones . " <p> That was changing rapidly , for better and worse . By 2014 , Americans had passed an important threshold : More young adults owned smartphones than computers , research shows , and social media use was soaring . <p> A new generation of students was " more willing than earlier generations to speak up about their perceived areas of injustice or unfairness , " said Khurana , the former undergraduate dean . Social media allowed them to express ways their classmates or universities made them feel like outsiders -- to raise awareness and demand better in a wider way . <p> In the spring of 2014 , a multimedia project called " I , Too , Am Harvard " showed up first on Tumblr , and then went viral after being picked up by BuzzFeed and other news sites . <p> Carol Powell/Tumblr <p> Created by a student , Kimiko Matsuda-Lawrence , the project included dozens of Black students holding placards that responded to hurtful comments they 'd heard at Harvard . <p> " Having an opinion does not make me an ' Angry Black Woman ' " read one . <p> Another student held a card that included the comment " I do n't see COLOR , " and asked " Does that mean you do n't see Me ? " <p> The project spread rapidly to other schools in the US -- " I , Too , Am NYU , " and " I , Too , Am Princeton " -- as well as universities in Canada and England . <p> Just a few months later , the power of social media was fully revealed . After the August 2014 police shooting of 18-year-old Michael Brown in Ferguson , Mo. , bystanders ' photos of his body posted on social media helped spread the Black Lives Matter movement nationwide . <p> Two opposing forces -- support for racial equality and a backlash to it -- emerged simultaneously , including on the Harvard campus . In 2015 , students organized a campaign to change the law school 's crest , which was linked to an 18th century family of slave owners who funded the school . Amid that call , vandals defaced framed portraits of Black faculty by placing black tape over their faces . <p> A 2014 " die-in " protest at Harvard Medical School , in response to the decision by authorities to not bring indictments in the police killings of Michael Brown in Ferguson , Mo. , and Eric Garner in New York . ( David L. Ryan/Globe Staff ) <p> " This is my portrait at Harvard Law School , " wrote Ronald Sullivan Jr . on Twitter , sending out a photo . He was one of 12 permanent full-time Black faculty at the school , out of 125 . The acts of vandalism were investigated as a hate crime and spurred the racial reckoning at the law school , which led to the crest being replaced . <p> As the 2015-16 academic year came to a close , it was clear to Harvard 's leaders that they still had important work to do to improve campus culture . Faust established a Presidential Task Force on Inclusion and Belonging , pulling together more than 50 faculty , staff , students , and alumni to work on solutions not just at the college , but at all of the many graduate and professional schools . <p> Danielle Allen , a professor of political philosophy , co-chaired the task force . Raised in a family with a prominent Black conservative father , she wanted it to address the needs of the university 's demographic groups , but also to go further . It should engage with the fact that politically conservative and religious students could feel marginalized on campus . <p> Allen reached out to a member of Harvard 's Republican student committee , Kent Haeffner , a varsity swimmer and a devout Christian . He 'd caught her attention by publicly criticizing the task force 's early decision to drop a reference to the Puritans from the school song , " Fair Harvard . " The university was founded in 1636 . Erasing its religious origins seemed absurd to Haeffner . <p> When they met in person , Haeffner said he was n't afraid to speak his mind , even on a campus dominated by liberal students . This was just the kind of perspective Allen knew Harvard needed . <h> Pranking Trump <p> The perception that the Harvard community was overwhelmingly liberal was not an exaggeration . <p> In 2016 , about 68 percent of the graduating seniors identified as " liberal " or " very liberal , " according to a survey by the Crimson , while just 8 percent said they were conservative or very conservative . Political moderates made up 22 percent , and 2 percent of respondents said they were apolitical . <p> There were signs the balance was even further tilted away from conservatives among faculty , instructors , and researchers . Between 2011 and 2014 , a separate Crimson analysis found , 84 percent of federal contributions from those groups went to Democratic campaigns and political action committees . The number rose to 96 percent among people affiliated with the faculty of Arts and Sciences . <p> After Trump announced his presidential bid in June 2015 , plenty of people at Harvard found the idea of him winning unimaginable . The student Republican club later withheld its endorsement of Trump , declining to support a GOP candidate for the first time since 1888 . " The rhetoric he espouses -- from racist slander to misogynistic taunts -- is not consistent with our conservative principles , " the group said . <p> Others at Harvard showed their disbelief in a different way , pulling off an epic prank . <p> In the summer of 2015 , writers for the Lampoon , the student humor publication , reached out to Trump 's campaign posing as Crimson staff . Tom Waddick , then 20 , said they 'd like to come to Manhattan and snap a photo of Trump sitting in the Crimson president 's special , throne-like chair , to go with an endorsement of him for president . The campaign agreed . <p> On the appointed day , Lampoon members hauled the chair -- temporarily liberated from the Crimson 's office -- into Trump Tower in Manhattan . Trump turned on the charm , saying they could touch his hair if they wanted to prove it was real . If they wanted him to speak at Harvard , he said , he 'd waive his hefty fee -- that was " a very good deal , " he noted . <p> " It was like he was there to entertain us , " recalled Waddick , now 31 , who grew up in Waltham and is presently a writer in Los Angeles . With unwitting campaign staff looking on , everyone posed for the picture giving Trump 's signature thumbs up . <p> Members of the Harvard Lampoon traveled to Trump Tower to pose with presidential candidate Donald Trump . They 'd convinced his campaign they were from the Harvard student newspaper , which they said would endorse him . Todd Waddick was standing at the immediate left of the chair , over Trump 's right shoulder . <p> Soon after the fake endorsement went up on a fake Crimson webpage , Waddick 's cellphone rang . It was Michael Cohen , Trump 's lawyer , yelling . He threatened to come to Cambridge himself , to make sure every student involved was expelled . <p> Looking back , Waddick said he got a preview of the future Trump administration 's bullying tactics . " Sad to say , it often works , " he said . The Lampoon agreed to take the site down . <p> Trump did n't say anything publicly about the prank , though spokesperson Hope Hicks issued a statement . " The students who perpetrated this are fraudsters and liars , but frankly it was a waste of only a few minutes , " it said . " Mr. Trump attended the great Wharton School of Finance , a school that has more important things to do . " <p> Trump also had more important things to do , like winning a presidential election . <p> At packed political rallies in oft-overlooked parts of the country , he tapped into authentic populist anger , speaking out against global trade agreements and championing issues embraced by evangelical Christians . With the help of political strategist Steve Bannon , he also leaned into anti-immigration messages , including his vows to ban Muslims and build a border wall to keep out Mexicans . <p> The morning after Trump 's victory , students in Harvard Yard moved in slow motion -- dazed , disbelieving , and , in many cases , devastated . <p> " I feel like it 's a nightmare that just came true , " one told the Crimson . <p> In his role as dean , Khurana typed an email to undergraduates . He tried to speak to all of them , whatever their political leanings . " In spite of our differences , " he wrote , " we can only move forward as friends , neighbors , and classmates if we develop the capacity to understand and empathize with each other . " <p> It was a hopeful message , but aspirational language could only do so much to bring people together . <p> " We were trying to do something difficult , " Khurana said this fall . " Something that the country has n't figured out . " <h> Defining diversity <p> On campus , Harvard 's leaders remained fully committed to diversifying their student body , including by expanding access across socio-economic lines . They believed these students should also feel they belonged on a campus where plenty of classmates had trust funds and vacation homes . <p> Harvard students held signs before a rally in January of 2017 , which included asking the university to protect undocumented students and Muslim students . ( Jessica Rinaldi/Globe Staff ) <p> By this time , roughly 15 percent of Harvardundergraduates were the first in their families to go to college , and more than half received full or partial financial aid . ( Today , Harvard reports that roughly one in four attend for free based on financial eligibility . ) <p> In some quarters , Harvard 's all-male final clubs were seen as perpetuating a culture of exclusivity that needed addressing . The private social societies , some dating back to the 1800s and housed in historic buildings around campus , enjoyed generations of alumni support . They also brought instant connections to elite careers in finance , tech , and consulting that are perennially popular among Harvard students . <p> Starting in 2017 , Harvard administrators , led by president Faust and Khurana , pressed the clubs to admit women . The sanctions they imposed were strict : Members would be barred from captaining universitysports teams and receiving endorsements for fellowships . <p> To Khurana , it seemed like a common sense decision . To others , the university was overreaching . One of Khurana 's predecessors as dean , Harry R. Lewis , urged him to pull back . " The College responds to improper acts , not memberships , " Lewis wrote him in a private letter . <p> The final clubs ultimately prevailed in getting the administration to rescind its sanctions , after a legal ruling in a similar matter hurt Harvard 's position . Still , some donors and alumni felt troubled by what they saw as the university passing sweeping moral judgment on the clubs . <p> The scene at the Fly Club , one of the all-male final clubs at Harvard , on May 7 , 2016 . ( Katherine Taylor/New York Times ) <p> Questions about Harvard 's leadership also surfaced for Ackman , the New York City hedge fund manager and major Harvard donor . The Harvard he remembered so fondly was one of stimulating classes and invigorating crew races on the Charles . But it was now seeming more like an indoctrination factory . <p> Ackman told the Globe his daughter became fascinated with Marxism during her time on campus in the late 2010s . " She came out of Harvard with a very negative view of capitalism generally , " he recalled . " She 'd get incredibly frustrated and upset with me . " <p> He said she began to sympathize with a worldview that largely cast America as a capitalist " oppressor " that victimizes other " oppressed " countries . <p> Today , Ackman said , he believes these kinds of binaries contributed to a campus environment where hateful speech toward groups seen as oppressors could seem justified . <p> " An oppressor-oppressed framework is a framework of resentment , " he said , " where the perception of success is an ill-gotten thing that was only achieved at the expense of someone else . " <p> Around this time , a number of conservative students raised similar concerns . May Mailman , a 2015 law school graduate who would rise quickly in the Trump administration , told the Globe that she saw elite universities including Harvard " glorifying victimization " in a way that stifled free speech and contrary views . <p> But many pushed back on this depiction , saying they are of a generation of minority groups willing to speak up -- and help inform others -- about comments or views that offend . And some have observed that others who demand a blanket right to free speech can use it as a license to say anything they want , no matter how offensive . <p> Noah Harris , a former Harvard student class president who is Black , watched these debates play out during his undergraduate years from 2018 to 2022 . " I do n't believe that every single person who was advocating for free speech at the time had problematic views , " he said . But among them , there were some who used free speech " as almost a shield for problematic ideas . " <p> These challenges came into full view as the politics around Israel sharpened . Several decades ago , the relationship between pro-Israel and pro-Palestinian students at Harvard had been fairly cooperative , including sometimes holding joint programs . But as armed conflicts in the region grew in the 2000s , the relationship between the two groups on campus frayed , according to two major task force reports Harvard released in 2025 . One was on combatting antisemitism and anti-Israel bias , and the other on fighting bias against Muslims , Arabs , and Palestinians . <p> In 2017 , the Palestine Solidarity Committee , a campus group , helped produce a public art installation called the " Wall of Resistance , " set up outside Harvard 's Science Center . The annual project began as a way to show humanitarian suffering broadly . Over time , it focused more on the plight ofPalestinians , with messages like " Zionism is Racism Settler Colonialism White Supremacy Apartheid . " <p> Some Jewish students , their numbers on campus declining in recent decades , felt their concerns about mounting anti-Israel messages on campus were being downplayed by the university administration , according to the antisemitism report . <p> " Every minority group is allowed to define what they consider to be discrimination , but when Jews deem something antisemitic , people do n't take that seriously , " a Jewish student wrote on the Hillel website . <p> Advertisement <p> Meanwhile , support for the Palestinian cause on campus grew , including fromstudents of Middle Eastern , South Asian , and African heritage , some of whom were moved by parallels to their own families ' experiences with mass displacement or Western imperialism . They were joined by other students criticizing Israel 's actions in the West Bank and the blockade of Gaza . <p> Some of these Harvard community members told the task force on bias against Palestinians that their views were being suppressed on campus , which they attributed to pressure from major donors with pro-Israeli views . " I 've never been told by the university I ca n't speak up . But it 's clear it 's different with Palestine issues , " one faculty member said . " The double standards are disheartening . " <h> ' Unchecked emotion ' <p> The leaders of the Inclusion and Belonging task force had hoped to have a broader impact when it released its final report in March 2018 . In retrospect , Allen , the co-chair , said they " did n't put enough bright arrows at the places where we were trying to drive change . " <p> The document was wide ranging in its recommendations , including bringing in more diverse faculty , building a " culture of mutual respect , " and creating more inclusive signage on campus . It also made a point of including " political outlook " as a type of diversity that Harvard should foster . <p> But Allen said the administration did n't end up taking serious steps toward cultivating viewpoint diversity . Instead , she said , the university 's priorities became influenced by national events , especially the surging Black Lives Matter movement that concentrated attention on racial injustice . <p> Kent Haeffner , in the back row left , with other members of the Harvard Republican Club , at a Jeb Bush town hall event in New Hampshire in September 2015 . ( Kent Haeffner ) <p> Haeffner , the Republican Club president , found participating on the task force a positive and eye-opening experience . But it did n't seem to him that promoting dialogue on campus had been a priority , either . What was really needed , he said , was helping students gain skills to constructively engage with ideas they find off-putting . <p> " It 's not enough just to say : ' Hey , you have free speech , ' " said Haeffner , now a consultant in Chicago . " Harvard 's mission is to train the future citizen leaders of the world . And how are you going to be able to train them if we ca n't get them comfortable being exposed to viewpoints different than their own ? " <p> The inclusion report did not deal with one crucial subject at all : how profoundly social media 's frenetic , polarizing churn was affecting campus interactions . <p> Looking back , Faust told the Globe this year that the most underappreciated cultural force at work during her 11-year presidency was the rise of the iPhone and social media . " And it was happening so inexorably , yet so quietly , we did n't fully notice , " she said . " It 's like boiling the frog . " <p> In 2019 , social media helped fan the flames of a controversy related to Sullivan , the Harvard law professor . He had received support as one of the Black faculty of the law school whose portraits were defaced in 2015 . About four years later , though , he became the target of protest himself , when news ricocheted on social media that he was representing Harvey Weinstein , the Hollywood mogulaccused of raping or sexually harassing dozens of women . Weinstein 's case catalyzed the #MeToo movement . <p> A contingent of students loudly demanded Sullivan step down , not from the law school faculty , but from his position as the residential faculty dean of one of Harvard 's dormitories , a position he 'd held for a decade . They said undergraduate women might now feel uncomfortable bringing concerns to him about sexual assault , a campus problem under heightened scrutiny . <p> Khurana and Claudine Gay , then dean of the faculty of Arts and Sciences , both weighed in , and Sullivan was pushed out of the faculty dean 's role , with administrators citing " climate " issues at the dorm . <p> Sullivan later accused Harvard officials of launching a probe tinged with racial bias -- he and his wife were the first Black residential deans in Harvard 's history . And in an op-ed in The New York Times , he asserted that the administration had " capitulated to protesters . " <p> Harvard Law professor Ronald Sullivan , then representing Harvey Weinstein in his sexual assault case , entered court in New York on April 26 , 2019 . ( Richard Drew/Associated Press ) <p> For years , Harvard 's administrators had been talking about how to handle emotionally charged tensions around identity , the kind that can metastasize on social media . But responding quickly has never been Harvard 's strength , Khurana acknowledged . " Our job is to think slow , " he said . " And that was becoming increasingly incongruent with the world that we were moving into . " <h> Attacking elites <p> There were other signs that the national political winds were becoming less favorable to Harvard . <p> By 2021 , an affirmative action case against Harvard had been winding its way to the Supreme Court for years . Students For Fair Admissions , a nonprofit founded by conservative legal strategist Edward Blum , first filed the landmark lawsuit in 2014 , arguing that Harvard 's affirmative action policy discriminated against Asian-American applicants . <p> Trump 's Justice Department later backed Blum 's case and launched its own investigation . " No American should be denied admission to school because of their race , " then-Attorney General Jeff Sessions said in a 2018 statement . " As a recipient of taxpayer dollars , Harvard has a responsibility to conduct its admissions policy without racial discrimination . " <p> Edward Blum , president of Students for Fair Admissions , in Copley Square in 2018 . The group filed a lawsuit claiming Harvard discriminated in admissions . ( Jessica Rinaldi/Globe Staff ) <p> During the case , the university repeatedly contested the plaintiff 's findings and methodology . The trial judge sided with Harvard in 2019 and so did the appeals court in 2020 . <p> But in 2021 , the case landed at the conservative-leaning Supreme Court , which appeared likely to rule against Harvard . <p> There , on a national stage , lawyers for the plaintiffs argued that Harvard not only gave advantages to underrepresented minorities , but also prioritized some already-privileged groups . <p> Its analysis of undergraduate applicants from the classes of 2014 to 2019 found an overall admission rate of about 6 percent . But when you drilled down into different groups , the odds improved . Harvard admitted nearly 34 percent of legacy applicants , as well as 42 percent of students on a special list generally associated with children of current or prospective donors . About 47 percent of the children of faculty and staff got in . <p> It could all look unfair to those hoping to get into Harvard . The undergraduate class size had stayed fairly static for decades , so admissions was essentially a zero-sum game : Advantages to one group took away from the others . And for many , admission policies like these were just one of the many ways the higher education system -- and the nation 's institutions in general - felt skewed against them . <p> As the case played out in court , there would be other stark reminders of societal divides . The COVID-19 pandemic exposed painful class divisions and the Jan. 6 Capitol riot -- the 2021 siege by Trump supporters claiming election fraud in his loss to Joe Biden -- was a sign of just how deep anger ran . <p> Among Trump 's backers questioning the election results was Representative Stefanik , a former moderate Republican who became a staunch Trump ally . As she perpetuated Trump 's claims of fraud , hundreds of students and alumni called on Harvard to cut its ties with her . The Harvard Institute of Politics , a program encouraging students to pursue public service , removed her from its senior advisory committee . <p> To Stefanik , who had been heavily involved at the institutesince her college days , this was just the latest example of Harvard silencing conservative voices . She blasted the organization for " caving to the woke Far-Left . " <h> Warring words <p> The Jan. 6 riot sounded a warning to the pillars of progressive society that the country was profoundly cleaving over race , class , and politics . Harvard doubled down on its inclusive mission . <p> In May 2017 , Harvard graduates took part in the Black Commencement ceremony , a special event during the graduation festivities . ( Keith Bedford/Globe staff ) <p> Bacow , who succeeded Faust as president in 2018 and long championed diversity efforts , put $5 million into a university-wide project to study Harvard 's ties to slavery . In announcing the initiative in November 2019 , he said Harvard has an obligation to understand the school 's past " from the ways the university benefitted from the Atlantic slave trade to the debates and advocacy for abolition on campus . " <p> Over this period , Harvard also continued to promote its central diversity office , to offer support to students and faculty , and to the units that handle bias complaints at the university 's schools . Academic departments began requiring applicants for faculty positions to submit " diversity statements , " asking them to articulate how they would support equity and inclusion efforts on campus . <p> By the summer of 2021 , another instructor on campus found herself at the center of political controversy . That July on " Fox and Friends , " Carole Hooven , a longtime lecturer in Harvard 's human evolutionary biology department , was asked to respond to news that some in medical schools felt pressure to use trans-inclusive terms , such as " pregnant people " rather than " pregnant women . " <p> Hooven was frustrated by how " ideology has been infiltrating science , " she said on the news show . " The facts are that there are , in fact , two sexes , " she continued . " There are male and female , and those sexes are designated by the kinds of gametes we produce . " <p> However , science and empathy were n't mutually exclusive , Hooven added . " We can treat people with respect and respect their gender identities and use their preferred pronouns , " she said , " so understanding the facts about biology does n't prevent us from treating people with respect . " <p> Fox News <p> The interview outraged Laura Simone Lewis , a graduate student in Hooven 's department and director of its diversity and inclusion task force . She tweeted a clip of Hooven 's TV interview with a message : " I am appalled and frustrated by the transphobic and harmful remarks made by a member of my dept in this interview with Fox and Friends . " <p> Hooven was surprised ; she and Lewis had a cordial relationship . She responded , also on Twitter : " I appreciate your concerns . Could you let me ( and the Twitterverse ) know exactly what I said that you consider transphobic or harmful to undergrads ? I think you know that I care deeply about all of my students , and I also care about science . How about a discussion ? " <p> The Twitter exchange spiraled from there , with others piling on . Hooven had many defenders , but within months , not a single graduate student would agree tohelp teach her course on the role of hormones in behavior , one of the university 's most popular . <p> Hooven had asked top administrators to publicly back her right to speak freely . They never lent her their full support , she said . In early 2023 , she felt her only choice was to leave the job she had loved for two decades . <p> " This is the thing that I can not get over to this day , " Hooven said in an interview with the Globe . " I assumed that the faculty and the administration would have my back . " <p> Hooven 's case was a tipping point for some Harvard faculty concerned about the chilling of speech on campus , an issue some believed was well within Harvard 's control to help fix . They organized the Council on Academic Freedom to promote civil discourse and viewpoint diversity . It drew in some prominent professors who had been outspoken on the issue in the past , such as Steven Pinker of the psychology department , Sullivan of the law school , and Tarek Masoud of the Kennedy School . <p> Masoud told the Globe that students need to know that a robust university education requires feeling some degree of discomfort . He said political analyst Van Jones put it well when he likened college learning to working out at a gym . <p> " Look , this is n't your home . Home is where you feel totally comfortable . You kick off your shoes , you watch too much Netflix , eat some chocolate , " Masoud said . " This is the gym . You 're not going to get stronger at the gym unless you make yourself uncomfortable by doing things like lifting heavy weights . <p> " You 're not going to get anything out of Harvard if you 're always comfortable here . " <p> On July 1 , 2023 , Harvard would get a new president , Claudine Gay , a prominent academic who was hailed for being dedicated to both campus diversity and free speech . " She has a bedrock commitment to free inquiry and expression , as well as a deep appreciation for the diverse voices and views that are the lifeblood of a university community , " said Penny Pritzker , head of the Harvard Corporation , the university 's top governing board . <p> Gay , the daughter of Haitian immigrants , would also be Harvard 's first Black president . And little would be easy about her tenure : Just two days before taking office , the US Supreme Court struck down Harvard 's race-conscious admissions policy . The court 's decision would require changes , she later said , but Harvard 's commitment to diversity " remains steadfast . " <h> The right rises <p> Trump 's movement did not sputter out after he left office in 2021 . The more progressive leaders pushed for their ideals , the harder the right pushed back with a fundamentally different vision of America 's future . <p> As Trump and his allies contemplated their political comeback , they seized on the idea of American cultural decline . Bannon , Trump 's former political strategist and a Harvard Business School graduate , had been fascinated by Hungary , where Prime Minister Viktor Orban set in a motion a series of events to crush liberal universities . <p> " What matters is the survival of the Judeo-Christian West , " Bannon told a crowd in Budapest in 2018 . " The West does not have to decline . This is not a law of physics . It can be reversed . " <p> The conservative activist Christopher Rufo in Tacoma , Wash. , on April 19 , 2022 . ( Chona Kasinger/New York Times ) <p> Another powerful new voice countering the DEI movement was Christopher Rufo , a former filmmaker and conservative writer . He earned a master 's in government at the Harvard Extension School , part of the university 's continuing education department . <p> He seized on a term in scholarly writing , " critical race theory , " and deployed it to describe the work of race-conscious initiatives within corporate HR departments and universities across the country . <p> In the fall of 2021 , an up-and-coming politician focused on higher education at the National Conservatism Conference.JD Vance , a Yale Law-educated Ohio candidate for the US Senate , gave a closing speech titled : " The universities are the enemy . " <p> Vance said universities had become " very hostile institutions " that were pushing DEI mandates , treatments for transgender youth , and training young women to prioritize career over family . <p> " If any of us want to do the things that we want to do for our country , and for the people who live in it , " he said , " we have to honestly and aggressively attack the universities in this country . " <h> October 7th <p> Violet Barron , a sophomore at Harvard , was up late studying in her Adams House dorm room on Oct. 7 , 2023 , when a news alert pinged her phone . Hamas-led militants had stormed into Israeli towns , murdering civilians and taking an untold number of hostages . <p> Barron cried as she scrolled the news online . For comfort in the days to come , she sometimes sang to herself a traditional Hebrew healing prayer , Mi Shebeirach . " I was scared for Israel , " the place whereshehad her Bat Mitzvah , she recalled recently . <p> Ever since Barron was little , growing up outside Los Angeles , she wanted to go to Harvard , just like her father and grandfather . Her first-year experience was similar to her dad 's : great classes and extra-curricular activities and new friends . People did n't always know she was Jewish -- she is biracial , with a Chinese-American mother -- but Judaism from her father 's side meant a lot to her . <p> Barron was among the many people across the political spectrum who were disgusted by a statement posted on Instagram , within hours of the Oct. 7th attack . Signed by the Harvard Undergraduate Palestine Solidarity Committee and more than 30 other campus groups , it blamed Israel for provoking the attack . <p> Instagram <p> " We , the undersigned student organizations , hold the Israeli regime entirely responsible for all unfolding violence , " the statement began . " Today 's events did not occur in a vacuum . For the last two decades , millions of Palestinians in Gaza have been forced to live in an open-air prison . " It went on to warn of a catastrophic counterattack by Israel . <p> The student groups ' statement was widely condemned . <p> " There was n't even 24 hours of sympathy on the Harvard campus for 1,200 Israelis being murdered , raped , killed , taken hostage , " Ackman , who is Jewish , recalled to the Globe . <p> Maya Bodnick , a Jewish undergrad , pushed back on the suggestion that the attack was somehow bound to happen because of Israel 's treatment of Palestinians . " This was a massacre ! It was n't inevitable , " she said to her boyfriend , who was Muslim , as she later recounted in a Globe essay . Nothing justifies " slaughtering over a thousand Jews . " <p> Two days later , Gay and other leaders put out a statement on " the war in Israel and Gaza now underway , " only to see it criticized by some for being too even-handed and late . She issued her own statement a day later , condemning the " terrorist atrocities perpetrated by Hamas . " But by then the damage was done . <p> Ackman called on Harvard to release names of those in the student groups , saying future employers had a right to know the type of people they were thinking of hiring . <p> A few days after the Oct. 7 attack , Barron saw a truck parked in Harvard Square . It displayed huge photos of students allegedly aligned with the group statement , labeling them " Harvard 's Leading Antisemites . " The conservative group behind the truck , Accuracy in Media , was also setting up websites in the names of protesters that included their personal information , exposing them to threats . <p> The doxxing of students stunned Barron . It made her want to know more about what those students thought and how they felt . She plunged into deeper reading about the Israeli-Palestinian conflict , but from a perspective she had never been taught growing up in America , the Palestinian point of view . <p> Reports of antisemitic comments and shunning on campus were alarming Jewish communities at Harvard , Columbia , Massachusetts Institute of Technology , and other schools . On Sidechat , a social media service popular on campuses , anonymous posts reportedly included anti-Israeli messages like " I proudly accept the label of terrorist . " The university increased security at the Harvard Hillel building . <p> Controversy erupted again on Oct. 18 , when an Israeli-American student on the Harvard Business School lawn began using his phone to film protesters at an anti-Israel " die-in . " Some worried his images would end up on doxxing trucks , which had appeared in Cambridge the week before . <p> During an Oct. 18 , 2023 , pro-Palestinian demonstration at Harvard Business School , protesters try to block a man from filming on his phone . ( Pat Greenhouse/Globe Staff ) <p> Protesters surrounded him , trying to block him from filming with their keffiyehs , and there was some jostling and physical contact . When Garber , Harvard 's provost , reviewed video of the incident , he seemed uncertain aboutwho was most responsible for escalating it . The student " was technically within his rights " to film there , and yet the " way he was taking videos appears provocative , " according to a text he sent to a colleague , which was obtained by a congressional committee . <p> The interaction was complex , but social media rarely allows for nuance . @@132772761 <p> Truckloads of fresh fruits and vegetables pass through Nogales , Arizona , every day , forming one of the busiest produce corridors in the United States . <p> Billions of pounds of tomatoes , cucumbers , squash , peppers and grapes move through warehouses along the border each year , shaping an economy built on the flow of food north . <p> Yet despite this abundance , much of the produce never reaches grocery stores . @@132780566 <h> Vehicle-To-Home Charging Shown To Save EV Owners Up To 90% <p> The perks to owning an electric vehicle are numerous and go beyond the obvious reduced fuel expenses and zero emissions . They are quiet and fast , with almost instant acceleration due to instant torque . They often require less maintenance because electric motors have fewer moving parts than the motors in internal combustion engine vehicles , and of course , you have the knowledge that you 're helping to reduce our dependence on fossil fuels and combating climate change . But did you know that you can also use some electric vehicles to power your home ? <p> It 's called vehicle-to-home ( V2H ) charging , and not every EV offers this feature . It sounds a bit like something out of " The Jetsons " or a Pixar movie , but it 's technology that we 're already living with ! EVs have massive batteries that could provide backup power to your home during a storm or simply as less expensive energy during those peak hours when your electric company is charging top dollar . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ both the appropriate hardware and software , are capable of performing this feat , and it 's often an optional add-on . Bi-directional charging is available on Ford 's F-150 Lightning , Kia 's EV9 , the Hyundai IONIQ 9 , Acura 's 2026 RSX , the 2026 Chevy Bolt , and a handful of others . <p> Vehicle-to-home charging is exactly what it sounds like : you essentially tap into the energy from your EV 's batteries just like you would a home generator , but without burning any gasoline . A new study by the University of Michigan and Ford Motor Co. found that the process has the potential to save owners thousands of dollars . <h> The potential of V2H <p> RossHelen/Shutterstock <p> Most automakers advertise V2H as something you can fall back on in an emergency , powering your home if the lights go out due to a storm or blackout . The University of Michigan study , however , focused on how EV owners can both save money and reduce emissions by providing power to homes on a daily basis . Drivers can buy electricity @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ during the day when solar power is available , and store it in the car 's battery for use at a later time . <p> The study found that V2H could save EV owners 40% to 90% of their charging costs over the lifetime of their vehicle , because they 'd be saving on their electric bill at other times of the day . V2H can also reduce greenhouse gas emissions from your household 's electric use by up to 250% . <p> V2H is still a relatively new concept , and Parth Vaishnav , assistant professor at the U-M School for Environment and Sustainability , admits that " the discussion around V2H has been largely about its possibility and benefits in principle . " Many EVs are not capable of bidirectional charging , and the study did not consider the cost of the equipment necessary for V2H . But the possibility of a far-reaching impact is there , turning what is viewed by some as a downside to EV ownership -- having to charge the vehicle -- into a major plus .

First , it affects what 's happening deep beneath the ground in the mantle where magma is formed . <p> In places like Iceland , where the crust is pulling apart , hot rock moves toward the surface to fill the space . As it rises upward , the pressure drops , allowing it to melt and form magma . <p> Lava flows along a fissure of the Bardarbunga volcanic @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Nescher/Reuters ) <p> Water from melting ice runs off of Fallj ? kull glacier , one of Vatnaj ? kull 's glacier tongues , in 2021 . Plus : Why America 's Founding Fathers would be appalled by Trump 250 years later , and Edward Berenson 's The Trial of Madame Caillaux . <p> On this week 's episode of The David Frum Show , The Atlantic 's David Frum opens with his thoughts on the upcoming 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence . He examines the many actions President Donald Trump has taken that run counter to the ideals articulated in 1776 , and considers how the Founders ' constitutional genius may ultimately be what frustrates Trump 's attempt to consolidate power . <p> David is then joined by his Atlantic colleague Charlie Warzel , a staff writer and the host of the Galaxy Brain podcast , to discuss the temptations that come with launching a new podcast and the challenge of serving an audience that often rewards extreme content . Together , they talk about the responsibility that comes with hosting a podcast in a media environment that prizes clicks over truth . They also explore how conspiracy theorists have come to function as an alternate reality of " mainstream media , " and why the fight for truth may not yet be lost . <p> Finally , David closes with a discussion of Edward Berenson 's The Trial of Madame Caillaux and what it reveals about how future generations may come to view our own beliefs . <p> <p> The following is a transcript of the episode : <p> David Frum : Hello , and welcome to The David Frum Show . I 'm David Frum , a staff writer at The Atlantic . My guest this week will be my Atlantic colleague , Charlie Warzel , the host of the Galaxy Brain podcast , and we 'll be talking about our experiences as new podcast hosts . We both launched podcasts this year . Some of the temptations , some of the dangers , and some of the lessons that we have learned from this year in podcasting . My book this week will be a 1992 history book , The Trial of Madame Caillaux , a study of a sensational sex and murder trial in pre -- World War I France . But before getting to either of those things , I want to open with some end-of-year thoughts as we conclude 2025 and move into 2026. 2026 , of course , is the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence , in 1776 , and is a powerful anniversary symbol in the American mind . As we move into this year , there are so many things that are going to be memorable and important and wonderful to celebrate . There are also some things happening that are really weird . One of the weirdest of them is a press release by the U.S. Mint just a few weeks ago . They are considering honoring the 250th anniversary of American independence with a set of commemorative , or dollar coins , featuring the image of President Donald Trump . <p> Now , it ' ' s not literally unprecedented for the United States to put living people on the coinage . It 's not even totally unprecedented for them to put living politicians on the coinage . The first dollar bill had the face of Salman Chase , Secretary of the Treasury in Lincoln ' ' s Cabinet , on the dollar bill . Salman Chase was a famous egomaniac . One of his contemporary colleagues in the Republican Party said , He 's an excellent man . I think that 's the quote . He 's an excellent man , but he 's got the delusion that the Christian Trinity has four persons in it instead of three , the fourth being Salman Chase himself . So it ' ' s not unprecedented . There may be other examples as well , but it is strange and shocking at any time for a living person , and especially a living president , to propose to put himself on the coinage of the money of the United States . And if a Founding Father saw that , I think they would be kind of startled . They would be more startled , however , at some more serious things that are happening . <p> Some things that actually , unlike the dollar coin , which is just a project , have already happened in the year 2025 . We have seen the president of the United States impose taxes at his sole volition . The Trump Treasury Department issued a release a few days ago that boasted that they had collected $200 billion in tariffs over the year 2025 . That 's $200 billion of taxes not authorized by Congress and a flagrant violation of the ideas and literal language of Article 1 of the Constitution , which puts both taxes and tariffs in the hands of Congress . The president and his team are proposing to spend that $200 billion . They 've had many ideas about how to spend it . Maybe they should give the money to the farmers . Maybe there should be a tax rebate . Maybe they should do something else . But all of those ideas for spending or tax rebates , again , all of those are congressional authority that the president is arrogating to himself -- something else that would have startled the founders of the country all those 250 years ago . <p> We 've seen the growth of an enormous federal police force , ICE , which has recruited and seems to take orders not from any kind of institution of law but from , again , a small team around the president , an almost personal police force of a kind that the United States has not seen before , certainly not on such a scale . And carrying out actions that , again , would have seemed unimaginable only a little while ago . Mass roundups without any kind of due process ; mass deportations . Deportation , of course , is a total presidential authority , but usually there 's some kind of hearing . And , of course , until now , you almost always -- the deported person is sent back to the place the deported person came from , not to a third country to which they had no contact , and not under conditions that are tantamount to torture or at least serious human-rights abuse . You would send them home . It 's not a crime to be illegally present in the United States . It 's a violation of the law , but it 's not something that you should be tortured for . You should be put on a plane , given a hot meal , and warned , Do n't come back , you 're breaking the rules . We 've seen the rise of presidential retaliation against media institutions using the regulatory apparatus of the state , regulatory apparatus that belongs to everybody , not just to him . And then using those same grants of threats , grants of regulatory favors or threats of the withholding of regulatory favors , to rearrange or redirect existing media companies to be more favorable to him , sometimes successfully , sometimes less so , but always with a kind of intent that would have seemed very sinister from the point of view of the founders of the American Republic . And we have seen , maybe most disturbing of all , the use of presidential war powers without any involvement of any kind of legal authority , any kind of congressional authority . We 're on the cusp , apparently , of some kind of military action against Venezuela -- maybe airstrikes , maybe clandestine strikes of commandos , maybe something more . There 's no pretense that there 's any congressional authorization of that . And over the Christmas holiday , the president fired missiles into Nigeria , intervening in Nigerian civil strife , again , with no pretense of any kind of authorization by anyone other than the president at his own whim . So the big question for the year 2026 is : How far has the country drifted from those ideals of 1776 as formalized in the Constitution of 1787 and all the amendments afterwards ? And how does the United States move back to the country it intended to be at the beginning , that Americans believed it to be until very recently , and that I think most Americans still want it to be . <p> Now , here 's some good news . It does seem like over the course of 2025 , that these lawless actions have lost some of their impact and power . The bad guys seem to be losing a little political altitude as we move into 2026 . I do n't want to be overconfident about that . I do n't want to issue false promises . But it does seem like the ebb and flow of political power is not favoring those who want to use arbitrary power in the way they 've used it . Some examples : There does seem to be , in this second Trump term , a real loss of focus , an inability to keep the main thing the main thing . The battle over renaming the Kennedy Center the Trump Kennedy Center : That seems like a perfect example of something that any serious authoritarian president would not waste energy over . What does he care ? He 's staffed it with his cronies . They 're going to do the shows that he likes ; he 's gon na be able to blackball the people he does n't like . Does he really need to put his name on it ? Does he need to host the Kennedy Honors on prime-time television ? Is that really something that he needs to invest energy in ? And even the dollar coins , that just makes enemies . Why are you doing that ? What is the petty , pathetic need that makes you trade the substance of political power for these childish shows ? But that need is there and it 's a political fact , and it 's an expensive political fact -- and therefore for those who oppose the authoritarian project , a hopeful political fact . <p> But more substantially , two other things are happening that are really changing the political calculus as we move into the year 2026 . One is the weakening of the American economy . One of the things that any successful authoritarian knows is you have to get the economy right . People will put up with a lot if they 're feeling prosperous . As they enter 2026 , fewer and fewer Americans are feeling prosperous . Prices are rising ; job creation is stalling . The center of energy in the American economy is the **34;907;TOOLONG boom . That may continue , it may not , but through the rest of the economy , it 's trouble . Everywhere there 's signs of trouble : rising corporate bankruptcies , defaults on automobile loans . Americans are not feeling like Trump is thinking of them as he thinks of himself . Trump 1 , the theory seemed to be that the public would forgive Trump 's actions if he provided economic prosperity . Trump 2 , the president is actually actively attacking prosperity through his taxes and tariffs , through his immigration policy , shrinking the American population , shrinking the American workforce . And it seems like that 's his agenda . So what do you get for putting up with it ? Nothing , just a kick in the head . <p> But the last thing , and Michael Waldman and I discussed this earlier this year in an important podcast discussion : Trump has lost much of his bet to centralize the management of elections in his own hands . Not all of the bet . He 's still got tricks up his sleeve . There are many things he 's trying to do . But through the genius of American federalism , which is part of the genius of 1776 and 1787 , election management is left in the hands of the state , of the several states . <p> And while it 's not impossible for a president to squeeze and coax and coerce and rig those elections , there are limits to his ability to do it . In the end , it is a state power governed by the actions of the states and administered by officials of the states . And there is a limit to how much the president can successfully intervene to corrupt or distort that process . Now , if the election is close , those interventions and distortions may be enough . <p> But when you have , through bad economic policy , you 've stoked so much discontent as this administration has , you may have moved the whole political temperature -- the whole political balance of political forces -- beyond the margin of successful manipulation . And that means that the corrective response , that the genius of the system always anticipated as the ultimate answer to abuses , that corrective response may be coming , and 2026 may be the year that we feel it . <p> And now , my dialogue with Charlie Warzel . <p> Music <p> Frum : So The Atlantic is , today , presenting something a little different .
